options: L = λ × W: average items in the system = arrival rate × average time in the system
Response time doubles when users double
questions.explanation: Little's Law relates average concurrency, throughput and time in system for any stable system.

questions.prompt: A service handles 50 requests per second with an average response time of 0.2 s. How many requests are in progress on average?
questions.code:
lam = 50   # req/s
W = 0.2    # s
L = lam * W

questions.prompt: For a closed load test, the number of virtual users needed depends on both response time and think time.
questions.explanation: Each user's cycle time is response time plus think time. Users = throughput × (response time + think time).

questions.prompt: You need 40 orders per second. Each user iteration takes 2 s of response time plus 8 s of think time and pacing. How many virtual users are required?
questions.explanation: N = X × (R + Z) = 40 × (2 + 8) = 400. Forgetting think time gives 80.

questions.prompt: A test runs 300 virtual users with 5 s think time. Response time is 1 s. What throughput should you expect, and what does it mean if you measure only 30 iterations/s?
options: About 50 iterations/s; measuring 30 means response time rose (to about 5 s) or users are blocked, so investigate
questions.explanation: X = N / (R + Z) = 300 / 6 = 50/s. At 30/s, R + Z = 10 s, so R ≈ 5 s, assuming think time is unchanged. The law gives a sanity check on test results.

questions.prompt: A connection pool must support 200 queries per second, each holding a connection for 25 ms on average. What is the minimum average number of busy connections?
questions.explanation: L = 200 × 0.025 = 5 connections busy on average. Size above this for bursts and variance.

questions.prompt: In an open-model test arriving at 100 req/s, response time climbs from 0.3 s to 6 s. What happens to concurrency in the system, and why does this matter?
options: It rises from about 30 to about 600 in-flight requests, which can exhaust threads, connections and memory and make things worse
It cannot change in an open model
questions.explanation: In an open model arrivals do not slow when the system does, so L = λW grows with W. That is why open-model tests expose collapse that closed-model tests can hide.

questions.prompt: A team claims their app server handles 1,000 concurrent users and has an average response time of 200 ms, while the load balancer shows 800 req/s. Assuming no think time, what does Little's Law say?
options: The figures are inconsistent: 1,000 in system at 0.2 s implies 5,000 req/s; at 800 req/s, 1,000 in system implies 1.25 s average time. One of the measurements is wrong or measured differently
Little's Law does not apply to web servers
questions.explanation: Little's Law is a cross-check between independently measured numbers. If they do not agree, something is mismeasured (e.g. users include idle sessions, or response time excludes queueing).

coding.title: Cross-check test results with Little's Law
coding.prompt:
Write `consistent(users, throughput, response_s, think_s, tolerance=0.1)` returning `True` if `users` is within `tolerance` (relative) of `throughput * (response_s + think_s)`, else `False`. Raise `ValueError` if throughput is not positive.

Example: `consistent(300, 50, 1, 5)` returns `True`; `consistent(300, 30, 1, 5)` returns `False`.
coding.explanation: If measured users, throughput and timings do not satisfy the law, something in the test is off: users stuck, think time not applied, or a timer measuring the wrong thing. This is a cheap automated sanity check for every run.
